questions.syllabus_ref: A1.3 Operating systems and control systems (A1.3.4 resource management, deadlock), A2.1 Network fundamentals
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.subtopic: A1.3 Operating systems and control systems
questions.challenge_mechanism: Deadlock is not a bug that shows up in testing but a structural property of the order in which resources are claimed, so the fix is a global ordering imposed on code that currently has none; the student has to see that adding a timeout does not remove the deadlock but merely converts it into repeated wasted work, and then quantify which is worse.

stimulus.title: Parcel packing cells
stimulus.body: A fulfilment centre runs four identical packing cells. Each cell processes one parcel per cycle of 45 s. Every parcel must pass through three shared resources, each of which can serve only one cell at a time: a labelling arm, a weighbridge and a dispatch chute. A cell claims the resources one at a time as its control program reaches each stage, holds every resource it has already claimed while it waits for the next, and releases them all only when the parcel has been dispatched. The three resources are attached to the site network so that any cell can request any of them. The centre currently achieves 320 parcels per hour when nothing goes wrong. On average, once in every 40 cycles the four cells deadlock: each holds one or two resources and waits for one held by another. There is no detection, so the deadlock persists until a supervisor notices the queue, walks to the cell, and performs a manual reset taking 6 minutes, which also discards the four parcels in flight. You have been asked to review the design.

questions.question: Using the case study, answer all four parts. The four cells are named C1 to C4 and the three resources are L (labelling arm), W (weighbridge) and D (dispatch chute).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, with reference to each of the four conditions required for deadlock, why this system deadlocks. Your answer must name all four conditions and show that each is present.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Construct a resource-allocation scheme that makes deadlock impossible. State the rule, show that it removes at least one of the four conditions you identified, and explain what has to change in the control program of each cell.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the average throughput of the centre in parcels per hour given the current deadlock rate, and hence the percentage of capacity lost. Show your working.

parts.label: d
parts.text: An engineer proposes instead to leave the resource requests unchanged and to add a timeout: any cell waiting more than 20 s releases everything it holds, waits 5 s and starts the parcel again. Evaluate this proposal against your scheme in (b).

questions.answer:
**(a)** All four Coffman conditions hold.

*Mutual exclusion:* each of L, W and D can serve only one cell at a time, so the resources are non-sharable. **(A1)**

*Hold and wait:* a cell that has claimed the labelling arm keeps it while it waits for the weighbridge, so processes hold resources while requesting others. **(A1)**

*No pre-emption:* nothing in the system can take a resource away from a cell; the only way resources are released is by the cell finishing, which is exactly what it cannot do. **(A1)**

*Circular wait:* with four cells and three resources a cycle is easy to form, for example C1 holds L and wants W, C2 holds W and wants D, and C3 holds D and wants L. Because each cell requests resources in whatever order its stage is reached, and the stages differ between parcels, no ordering prevents that cycle from forming. **(A1)**

**(b)** Impose a **global ordering on resource acquisition**: assign each resource a fixed rank, say L = 1, W = 2, D = 3, and require every cell to request resources in strictly increasing rank order, never requesting a lower-ranked resource while holding a higher-ranked one. **(M1)(A1)**

This removes the circular-wait condition. **(A1)** A cycle would require each participant to hold a resource and wait for one of lower or equal rank; since ranks strictly increase along any wait chain, the chain cannot close. Formally, in any cycle the ranks would have to satisfy $r_1 < r_2 < \dots < r_k < r_1$, which is impossible. **(A1)**

The control program must change in two ways: each cell must determine the full set of resources its parcel will need **before** claiming any of them, and must then claim them in rank order. Where a parcel genuinely needs them in a different order, the cell must claim all three up front and hold them for the whole cycle, which reduces concurrency but is safe. **(A1)**

**(c)** Without deadlock the centre does $4 \times \dfrac{3600}{45} = 320$ parcels per hour. **(A1)**

In 40 cycles the four cells process $4 \times 40 = 160$ parcels, taking $40 \times 45 = 1800\ \mathrm{s}$. One deadlock adds a 6-minute ($360\ \mathrm{s}$) reset, so 160 parcels take $1800 + 360 = 2160\ \mathrm{s}$. **(M1)(A1)**

$$\text{throughput} = \frac{160}{2160} \times 3600 = 266.7 \approx 267\ \mathrm{parcels\,h^{-1}}$$ **(A1)**

$$\text{loss} = \frac{320 - 267}{320} \times 100\% = 16.7\%$$

**(d)** The timeout does **not** prevent deadlock; it detects and breaks it. **(A1)** That is better than an indefinite hang, but it is worse than prevention in three respects. First, every near-deadlock costs 20 s of waiting plus a 5 s backoff plus the wasted work already done on the parcel, so each event costs at least 25 s of cell time against 0 s under ordering. Second, if all four cells time out together and restart together they are likely to re-form the same cycle, an effect known as livelock, which the proposal does nothing to prevent since there is no randomised backoff. **(A1)** Third, the parcels are discarded either way, so the material loss is unchanged. **(A1)**

By contrast the ordering scheme in (b) eliminates the events entirely, at the cost of holding all three resources for some parcels and so losing some concurrency. A reasonable evaluation is therefore that the timeout is an acceptable **safety net** to keep in place, but it should not be the primary mechanism: prevention should be used first and detection second.
questions.markscheme_notes: (a) Award one mark for each condition correctly named and shown to be present; a candidate who names all four but does not apply them to this system earns at most two. The circular-wait mark is the one most often missed and requires an explicit example of a cycle. (b) Accept any consistent global ordering, not necessarily L-W-D, provided the rule is stated as a total order and the reasoning about cycles is given. A candidate who proposes requesting all resources at once (simultaneous acquisition) is also acceptable and should be credited equivalently, since it removes the hold-and-wait condition instead; note in that case that utilisation falls. The final mark is for identifying the change to the control program, which is the practical consequence and is frequently omitted. (c) Accept 266 to 267 parcels per hour and a loss between 16% and 17%. Award the method mark for converting the deadlock rate into an amortised time penalty; a candidate who simply subtracts 6 minutes per hour has the wrong model. (d) The key distinction is prevention versus detection, and candidates who conflate them should not earn the first mark. Credit the livelock observation even if the term is not used, provided the idea that simultaneous restart recreates the cycle is stated. There is no single right conclusion, so award the final marks for a judgement supported by the analysis given.
questions.explanation:
Deadlock is one of the few topics in the syllabus where the correct answer is a property of the whole system rather than of any single piece of code. No individual cell's control program is wrong: each one claims a resource, uses it, and later asks for another. The fault is the absence of a global rule, which is why the question asks for all four Coffman conditions explicitly. Naming them is not rote learning here; it is the diagnostic that tells you which one is cheapest to remove. Mutual exclusion cannot be removed, because a weighbridge genuinely cannot serve two parcels at once. Hold-and-wait can be, by claiming everything up front, but that costs concurrency. Circular wait is the cheapest to break, because imposing an order on requests costs nothing in throughput and requires only that the program decide its requirements in advance.

The quantification in (c) is there to make the cost concrete, and the result is larger than most students expect: one deadlock every forty cycles costs a sixth of the centre's output, because a six-minute reset is eight full cycles lost. That reframes the decision. A fix that costs a little concurrency on every cycle is clearly worth buying against a one-in-forty chance of losing eight cycles.

Part (d) is where the question discriminates. Adding a timeout feels like a fix and is not one: it converts a permanent hang into a recurring 25-second penalty and, because all four cells are running the same cycle time and will therefore tend to time out together, it risks livelock where the system makes no progress at all despite no process being blocked. The mature answer is that prevention and detection are complementary, and that the ordering scheme should be primary with the timeout retained as a backstop. Recognising that a mechanism which breaks a deadlock is not the same as one that prevents it is the transferable idea.

provenance.adaptation: Original case study. The four-condition diagnosis, the ordering solution and the timeout alternative are standard operating-systems material; the resource set, cycle time, deadlock frequency and reset duration were chosen so that the amortised throughput loss is an exact sixth, and so that livelock from synchronised restart is a live risk.

verification.method: Throughput model recomputed in Python: 4 x 3600/45 = 320 parcels per hour clean; 160 parcels in 40 cycles taking 1800 s plus a 360 s reset gives 160/2160 x 3600 = 266.67 parcels per hour, a loss of 53.33 parcels per hour or 16.67 percent.
solution_skeleton: check each of the four deadlock conditions against the specific resource set
construct an explicit circular-wait cycle from the described request pattern
impose a total order on resource acquisition to break circular wait
amortise the deadlock recovery time over the cycles between events to get throughput
distinguish mechanisms that prevent deadlock from those that only detect it

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Add a timeout to each resource request so that a stalled process gives up and retries, and describe the deadlock as solved.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: Deadlock is a structural consequence of the order in which resources are claimed, so a timeout does not remove it; it converts a permanent stall into repeated wasted work, and only imposing one global order on the claims breaks the cycle.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: A timeout described as the fix, with throughput reported as unchanged and the circular wait left in place.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.syllabus_ref: A2.4 Network security, A1.2 Data representation and computer logic (binary, hexadecimal, hashing)
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.challenge_mechanism: The vulnerability is not that the lock's secret is weak but that the same bits are accepted every time, so the student has to see that freshness, not secrecy, is the missing property; the protocol then has to be built so that the response depends on a value the attacker cannot predict, and the evaluation has to confront that the fix costs almost nothing, which removes the usual excuse for shipping the weak version.

stimulus.title: Wireless smart lock
stimulus.body: A smart lock is fitted to a communal entrance. The lock is battery powered and communicates with the resident's phone over a short-range wireless link. The current protocol works as follows. The lock stores a 32-bit shared secret $S$. To unlock, the phone transmits a single frame containing the ASCII text OPEN followed by the 32-bit value $S$ in hexadecimal. The lock compares the received value with its stored $S$ and, if they match, releases the bolt. There is no encryption, no timestamp and no counter. An attacker with a $40\ \mathrm{EUR}$ software-defined radio can capture any frame transmitted within about $15\ \mathrm{m}$ and can later transmit arbitrary bytes. The lock is rated for $25$ operations per day on a $2.4\ \mathrm{Ah}$, $3.0\ \mathrm{V}$ battery. Its microcontroller can compute a keyed hash over $32$ bytes in $4\ \mathrm{ms}$ using $0.90\ \mathrm{mJ}$, whereas transmitting the current static frame costs $0.15\ \mathrm{mJ}$. The round-trip time on the wireless link is $40\ \mathrm{ms}$ and the bolt must be released within $250\ \mathrm{ms}$ of the resident's tap.

questions.question: You have been asked to redesign the protocol. Use the case study to answer all four parts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a replay attack against the current protocol. State exactly what the attacker captures, what they transmit, why the lock accepts it, and how long the attack remains available to them.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Construct a challenge-response protocol that prevents replay. Your answer must specify what the lock sends, what the phone computes, what the phone returns, and what the lock checks.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how your protocol defeats the replay attack, and state clearly one attack it does not defeat. Quantify the probability that an attacker who has captured a million previous exchanges could still succeed by guessing.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate whether the additional cost of your protocol is acceptable for a battery-powered lock. Your answer must include a calculated comparison.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The attacker positions the receiver within range and captures one legitimate frame, which contains the literal text OPEN followed by the 32-bit secret $S$ in hexadecimal. **(A1)** Because the frame is not encrypted, the attacker reads $S$ directly from the captured bytes; because nothing in the frame varies, no computation is needed at all. **(A1)**

To unlock later, the attacker retransmits exactly the captured bytes. The lock compares them with its stored $S$, finds them identical, and releases the bolt. **(A1)**

The attack remains available **indefinitely**, or until $S$ is changed, because the accepted value never varies and there is no timestamp, counter or expiry. Capturing one frame grants permanent access. **(A1)**

**(b)** Protocol:

1. The phone sends a request frame containing HELLO and its device identifier. **(A1)**
2. The lock generates a fresh 64-bit random value $N$ (a nonce) using its hardware random source, stores it with a short expiry, and transmits CHALLENGE followed by $N$. **(A1)(A1)**
3. The phone computes $R = H(S \mathbin\| N)$, where $H$ is a keyed hash and $\|$ denotes concatenation, and returns RESPONSE followed by $R$. **(A1)**
4. The lock computes the same value from its stored $S$ and the $N$ it issued, compares with $R$ using a constant-time comparison, and releases the bolt only if they match and $N$ has not expired or been used before. **(A1)**

**(c)** The captured bytes are now useless because each exchange uses a different $N$. A response $R$ valid for one nonce produces a completely different hash for the next, and the phone never transmits $S$ itself, so the attacker who captures a million exchanges has a million $(N_i, R_i)$ pairs but no way to recover $S$ or to compute the response to a nonce they have not seen. **(M1)(A1)**

It does **not** defeat an active man-in-the-middle who relays a challenge to the genuine phone and returns the genuine response, because the protocol authenticates the phone to the lock but not the lock to the phone, and it does not defeat physical attacks on the lock or compromise of the phone itself. **(A1)**

If the attacker instead tries to guess the next nonce, the chance that a 64-bit value repeats one seen before, by the birthday bound after $10^{6}$ exchanges, is approximately **(M1)**

$$\frac{N^{2}}{2^{65}} = \frac{10^{12}}{3.69\times10^{19}} \approx 2.7\times10^{-8},$$

that is, about one chance in forty million. **(A1)**

**(d)** The additional cost is negligible and the protocol is clearly acceptable. **(A1)** The extra energy per operation is $0.90 - 0.15 = 0.75\ \mathrm{mJ}$ for the hash plus a second transmission of about $0.15\ \mathrm{mJ}$, so about $0.90\ \mathrm{mJ}$ in total. At 25 operations per day that is **(M1)**

$$0.90\times10^{-3} \times 25 \times 365 = 8.2\ \mathrm{J}\ \text{per year}.$$

The battery stores $2.4\ \mathrm{Ah} \times 3600\ \mathrm{s} \times 3.0\ \mathrm{V} = 25\,920\ \mathrm{J}$, so the extra drain is **(A1)**

$$\frac{8.2}{25\,920} \times 100\% \approx 0.032\%\ \text{of capacity per year}.$$

On latency, the protocol adds one round trip of $40\ \mathrm{ms}$ to the $250\ \mathrm{ms}$ budget, leaving $210\ \mathrm{ms}$ for the hash and the bolt mechanism against the $4\ \mathrm{ms}$ the hash actually needs. **(A1)** The conclusion is that the security improvement is effectively free, so there is no engineering justification for shipping the static-token version.
questions.markscheme_notes: (a) Award the marks for capturing the frame, retransmitting it unchanged, the lock's equality check succeeding, and the indefinite lifetime of the attack. The last is the mark most often missed and is the reason the attack is severe rather than merely possible. (b) Accept any challenge-response design in which the lock supplies a fresh unpredictable value and the response depends on both that value and the shared secret. Credit equivalent constructions such as a counter-based scheme, but note that a counter requires synchronised state and ask what happens when it desynchronises. Do not credit a design in which the phone chooses the nonce unless it also signs it, since then the nonce provides no freshness guarantee to the lock. (c) The 'does not defeat' mark requires a specific named attack, not a vague statement that no system is perfectly secure; man-in-the-middle, physical tampering and phone compromise are all acceptable. For the probability, accept the birthday form $N^2/2^{65}$ or a simpler $10^6/2^{64}$ estimate, and accept any value of the order of $10^{-8}$ to $10^{-7}$. (d) The calculation must appear; a qualitative assertion that the cost is small earns nothing. Accept any reasonable energy model that uses the figures given, and credit a candidate who also notes that the hardware random source and the constant-time comparison are implementation requirements rather than automatic consequences of the design.
questions.explanation:
The instructive part of this question is that the secret is not weak. A 32-bit value has over four billion possibilities, and if the lock required the attacker to guess it, the attack would fail. The system is broken for a different reason: the same bits are accepted every single time. That makes the problem one of freshness rather than secrecy, and it is why no amount of lengthening the secret would help. A student who diagnoses the flaw as 'the secret is too short' has the wrong model and will propose a longer static token, which is exactly as vulnerable.

The fix follows from the diagnosis. If the value accepted must differ each time, then either the lock or the phone must contribute something new to every exchange, and the lock must be the one to do it, because a nonce chosen by the phone carries no freshness guarantee to the lock. Once the lock issues a random challenge, the phone's response can be a keyed hash over the secret and the challenge, which proves knowledge of $S$ without ever transmitting it. That last property matters more than it first appears: under the original protocol every transmission leaked the secret, so the system was one capture away from total compromise, whereas under the new one an attacker who records a million exchanges learns nothing reusable.

The evaluation in (d) is included because security questions in practice are decided on cost, and because the answer here is unusually clean. The extra energy is about three hundredths of one percent of the battery per year and the added latency is well inside the existing budget, so the secure protocol is effectively free. That removes the usual defence of a weak design, and a candidate who computes it has a much stronger argument than one who merely asserts that security is worth the cost. The part also asks what the protocol does not defeat, because a design that appears to solve everything is usually a design whose limits have not been thought about; here the absence of lock-to-phone authentication leaves a relay attack open, which is a real and documented vulnerability in systems of this kind.

provenance.adaptation: Original case study. The static-token vulnerability and the challenge-response remedy are standard; the device parameters were chosen so that the additional energy cost works out at roughly three hundredths of one percent of battery capacity per year, making the security trade-off numerically one-sided.

verification.method: Energy and latency model recomputed in Python: battery 2.4 Ah x 3600 s x 3.0 V = 25920 J; extra 0.90 mJ per operation at 25 per day gives 8.213 J per year, 0.0317 percent of capacity; birthday collision probability for 10^6 nonces over 64 bits computed as 10^12/2^65 = 2.71e-8; latency check 40 ms of a 250 ms budget.
solution_skeleton: identify the missing property as freshness rather than secrecy
have the verifier issue an unpredictable challenge before any response
bind the response to both the shared secret and the challenge with a keyed hash
bound the chance of an attacker reusing a captured exchange by the birthday bound
compare the added energy and latency against the device budget to judge the trade-off

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Strengthen the secret the lock and the reader share, and lengthen the code it produces, so that the response cannot be guessed.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The weakness is not the strength of the secret but that the same bits are accepted on every use, so a recorded exchange can be replayed whatever the secret is; the missing property is freshness rather than secrecy.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: A longer shared secret offered as the remedy, with the replay of a recorded exchange still possible and no value introduced that the attacker cannot predict.

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.syllabus_ref: A3.2 Database design, A3.3 Database programming, B1.1 Approaches to computational thinking
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.challenge_mechanism: The tempting answer is to rewrite the system, and the question is built so that the numbers make the incremental route obviously better: the student has to price both options, discover that a single failed cutover costs roughly fifteen times the entire dual-running programme, and then design the phasing so that the two systems can genuinely be reconciled while both are live.

stimulus.title: Migrating a policy administration system
stimulus.body: An insurer administers 18 million policy records on a forty-year-old mainframe system written in COBOL, with data held in flat files and indexed by a bespoke access method. The system processes 240 000 transactions per night in a batch window and about 3 200 payment instructions per hour during the day. It is reliable but there are four staff in the country who can maintain it, all within ten years of retirement. The board has approved a migration to a relational database behind a service interface. Two proposals are on the table. Proposal A is a big-bang cutover on a single weekend: the new system is built in full, the old one is switched off, and if the new system fails the fallback is to restore the mainframe from the previous night's backup, which takes 14 hours. Proposal B is an incremental migration in which a facade routes each function either to the old or the new system, functions are moved one at a time, and both systems run in parallel until the last one is moved. The migration team estimates that dual running costs EUR 14 000 per month in additional infrastructure and that a reconciliation mismatch rate of 0.02% is achievable, each exception taking an average of 6 minutes to investigate. Analyst time is costed at EUR 65 per hour.

questions.question: Using the case study, answer all four parts. Assume a month is 30 nights of batch processing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a big-bang cutover is a poor choice for this system, referring to specific figures in the case study rather than to general principles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Construct an incremental migration plan. State the mechanism that routes each request, the order in which you would move functions and why that order, and how the two systems are kept consistent while both are live.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of nine months of dual running, including the analyst time spent on reconciliation. Show your working.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate the two proposals. If a failed big-bang cutover causes an 8-hour outage in which 3 200 payments per hour are missed and each missed payment costs EUR 120 in penalties and remediation, compare that with your answer to (c) and state which proposal you recommend.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The decisive figure is the fallback: restoring from the previous night's backup takes 14 hours, during which roughly $14 \times 3200 \approx 45\,000$ payment instructions are not processed. **(A1)** A single failed cutover therefore risks a full working day of missed payments on a book of 18 million policies. **(A1)**

The staff position removes the option of a leisurely recovery. Only four people can maintain the old system, so if the new system fails and the old one must be restored and then kept running, there is almost no capacity to diagnose and fix the new one. **(A1)**

There is also no way to validate the new system at full scale before committing: 240 000 transactions per night cannot be simulated faithfully enough to be confident, and the first genuine run would also be the production run. **(A1)**

**(b)** *Mechanism:* place a **facade** in front of both systems. Every request arrives at the facade, which inspects the function being invoked and routes it either to the mainframe or to the new service. Callers never know which is serving them, so functions can be moved one at a time and moved back if necessary. **(M1)(A1)**

*Order:* move the **read-mostly reference functions first**, then simple queries, then writes, and leave the nightly batch and the payment instruction generation until last. **(A1)** The reason is that a read that goes wrong is visible immediately and is cheap to reverse, whereas a write that goes wrong corrupts data that may not be discovered for weeks; and the batch window is the most complex and least reversible part of the system, so it should be migrated only when everything feeding it is already new. **(A1)**

*Consistency while both are live:* run both systems for each migrated function and compare their outputs automatically every night, logging any disagreement as an exception for an analyst. The mainframe remains the system of record until a function has run clean for a sustained period, at which point the new system becomes the record for that function and the old one stops being authoritative for it. **(A1)**

**(c)** Infrastructure: $9 \times 14\,000 = \text{EUR }126\,000$. **(A1)**

Exceptions per night: $0.02\% \times 240\,000 = 48$. **(M1)**
Time per night: $48 \times 6 = 288$ minutes $= 4.8$ hours. **(A1)**
Over nine months, $9 \times 30 = 270$ nights: $270 \times 4.8 = 1296$ hours, at EUR 65 per hour:
$$1296 \times 65 = \text{EUR }84\,240$$
Total: $126\,000 + 84\,240 = \text{EUR }210\,240$. **(A1)**

**(d)** A failed cutover misses $8 \times 3200 = 25\,600$ payments, costing **(M1)**
$$25\,600 \times 120 = \text{EUR }3\,072\,000.$$
Comparing with the EUR 210 240 for nine months of dual running, a single failure costs about (A1)
$$\frac{3\,072\,000}{210\,240} \approx 15$$
times as much as the entire incremental programme. **(A1)**

**Recommendation: Proposal B.** Even if one assumed a failure probability for the big-bang cutover as low as one in ten, its expected cost would be about EUR 307 000, still above the full cost of dual running, and the incremental route has the further advantages of keeping the old system available as a live fallback for every function not yet moved, of building operational confidence gradually, and of allowing the four remaining experts to be consulted steadily rather than in a crisis. The one real drawback is the nine-month cost of running both, which the calculation shows to be small relative to the risk avoided.
questions.markscheme_notes: (a) The marks are for using the figures; general assertions about risk earn nothing. The 14-hour restore and the four maintainers are the two that matter most, and a candidate who cites only the size of the dataset has missed the point, since size alone is not the difficulty. (b) Award (M1) for the facade concept regardless of the name used; a candidate who proposes a hard switch per function without a routing layer has not solved the problem. The order mark requires a reason, and the reason must be about reversibility or blast radius rather than convenience. The consistency mark is for dual-running with automated comparison and a defined point at which authority transfers; a candidate who says the two databases are kept synchronised by replication should be asked how, given that the schemas differ. (c) Accept a total between EUR 200 000 and EUR 220 000 depending on the assumption about nights per month; award the method marks for the mismatch count and the conversion to cost. (d) The comparison must be quantitative. Credit a candidate who goes further and computes an expected value or a break-even failure probability, since that is the strongest form of the argument. A recommendation of Proposal A is not creditable given these figures, but a candidate who argues for a shorter dual-running period, say four months, on the grounds that the mismatch rate would fall as the new system stabilises, should be credited.
questions.explanation:
Migration questions are usually answered with principles: do it incrementally, keep a fallback, test thoroughly. Those are all true and none of them is an argument. This question is built so that the argument is arithmetic. The cost of nine months of dual running, including every exception being investigated by a human being, is a little over two hundred thousand euro. The cost of one failed cutover, priced at the contractual penalty per missed payment, is over three million. That is a factor of about fifteen, and it means the incremental route is not merely more cautious but cheaper even if you assume the big-bang would usually succeed.

The design part is where the real difficulty sits, and it is not the routing mechanism, which is straightforward. It is deciding the order. The principle is that the cost of being wrong should rise as slowly as possible, which means moving functions whose failure is immediately visible and cheaply reversed before functions whose failure is silent and expensive. Read-only reference data is the obvious first candidate: if the new system returns the wrong address, someone notices the same day and nothing is corrupted. Writes are the opposite. And the nightly batch, which is the most intricate part and the one whose failure is discovered last, must go last, when everything that feeds it has already been proven.

Keeping the two systems consistent is the part students underestimate. It is not enough to say the databases are synced; the schemas differ, the semantics of a forty-year-old flat-file system rarely map cleanly onto a relational model, and the only practical approach is to run both and compare the outputs, treating every disagreement as an exception to be investigated. That is why the reconciliation cost is built into the calculation rather than treated as an afterthought: the 0.02 percent mismatch rate is not a rounding error, it is forty-eight investigations a night for nine months, and any plan that ignores it is not a plan.

provenance.adaptation: Original case study. The figures were chosen so that the cost of a single failed cutover is almost exactly fifteen times the fully loaded nine-month cost of dual running, which makes the recommendation follow from the arithmetic rather than from a preference for caution.

verification.method: Cost model recomputed in Python: infrastructure 9 x 14000 = 126000; nightly exceptions 0.0002 x 240000 = 48; nightly analyst time 48 x 6 / 60 = 4.8 h; over 270 nights 1296 h at EUR 65 = EUR 84240; total EUR 210240; failed cutover 8 x 3200 x 120 = EUR 3072000; ratio 14.6.
solution_skeleton: price the failure mode of the abrupt option using the stated recovery time
introduce a routing layer so each function can be moved independently and reversed
order the moves by how visible and reversible a failure would be
dual-run and compare outputs to keep both systems consistent while both are live
compare the total incremental cost against the cost of one failure and recommend

questions.subject: Computer Science HL
questions.syllabus_ref: A4.1 Machine learning fundamentals, A4.4 Ethical considerations, A3.1 Database fundamentals
questions.topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
questions.challenge_mechanism: The model has better recall in the area that complains and much worse precision, so the aggregate figures look acceptable while the burden falls unequally; the student has to compute the rates separately for each group, notice that the headline number hides a fourfold difference, and then recognise that choosing which error to minimise is an ethical decision that no metric can settle.

stimulus.title: Prioritising housing repairs
stimulus.body: A local authority receives repair requests from tenants and must decide which to inspect within 48 hours. It has deployed a model that scores each request and flags those it predicts to be urgent. Urgent means a fault that is dangerous or that will cause rapid deterioration, such as a leaking roof or a failed heating system in winter. The authority covers two areas with very different housing stock. In the North area, of 6 000 requests in the period, 1 500 were genuinely urgent; the model flagged 1 200 as urgent and 1 080 of those were genuinely urgent. In the South area, of 2 000 requests, 400 were genuinely urgent; the model flagged 500 as urgent and 320 of those were genuinely urgent. The authority reports an overall precision of 82% and states that the model is therefore performing well. A tenant in the South area has complained that inspectors call on her neighbours repeatedly for faults that turn out to be minor, while her own leaking roof waited nine days.

questions.question: Using the case study, answer all four parts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the single figure of 82% overall precision is a misleading summary of this model's performance, and state which two quantities must be reported separately for the complaint to be assessed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Construct the confusion matrix for each area and calculate, for each area separately, the precision, the recall, and the proportion of non-urgent requests that were wrongly flagged.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss what the two sets of figures show, including anything they do not establish. Refer to the tenant's complaint in your answer.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Justify one action the authority should take, given that it cannot simultaneously maximise both precision and recall and that inspection capacity is fixed.

questions.answer:
**(a)** An overall figure averages over a population in which the two areas contribute very unequally, 6 000 requests from the North against 2 000 from the South, so the aggregate is dominated by the area where the model performs better. **(A1)** It says nothing about how the errors are distributed, and it is the distribution that the complaint is about. **(A1)**

The two quantities that must be reported separately are **precision and recall for each area**, or equivalently the false-positive rate and the false-negative rate for each area, since precision and recall alone do not determine how many non-urgent requests are wrongly flagged. **(A1)(A1)**

**(b)** *North:* flagged 1 200, of which 1 080 urgent, so 120 are not urgent. There are 1 500 urgent in total, so $1500 - 1080 = 420$ urgent requests were missed. Non-urgent requests number $6000 - 1500 = 4500$, of which 120 were wrongly flagged. **(M1)(A1)**

| North | flagged urgent | not flagged | total |
|---|---|---|---|
| genuinely urgent | 1 080 | 420 | 1 500 |
| not urgent | 120 | 4 380 | 4 500 |
| total | 1 200 | 4 800 | 6 000 |

*South:* flagged 500, of which 320 urgent, so 180 are not urgent. There are 400 urgent in total, so $400 - 320 = 80$ were missed. Non-urgent requests number $2000 - 400 = 1600$, of which 180 were wrongly flagged. **(A1)**

| South | flagged urgent | not flagged | total |
|---|---|---|---|
| genuinely urgent | 320 | 80 | 400 |
| not urgent | 180 | 1 420 | 1 600 |
| total | 500 | 1 500 | 2 000 |

North: precision $= 1080/1200 = 90.0\%$, recall $= 1080/1500 = 72.0\%$, wrongly flagged $= 120/4500 = 2.67\%$. **(A1)**
South: precision $= 320/500 = 64.0\%$, recall $= 320/400 = 80.0\%$, wrongly flagged $= 180/1600 = 11.25\%$. **(A1)**

**(c)** The figures support the substance of the complaint. A non-urgent request in the South is **(M1)**
$$\frac{11.25}{2.67} \approx 4.2$$
times as likely to be flagged as one in the North, so South tenants are much more likely to be visited for a fault that turns out to be minor, which is the nuisance she describes. **(A1)** At the same time the model is not uniformly worse in the South: its recall there is higher, 80% against 72%, so an urgent request in the South is more likely to be caught. That is why her own roof waiting nine days is not necessarily explained by the area statistics and may be a single unfortunate case. **(A1)**

What the figures do **not** establish is why the difference exists. The areas differ in housing stock, so the base rate of urgency differs, 25% in the North against 20% in the South, and a model trained on pooled data with one threshold will not behave identically across groups with different base rates even if it is free of bias in its inputs. The data also cannot distinguish a model that is miscalibrated from one that is correctly calibrated but operating at an inappropriate threshold, and they say nothing about whether the features used are themselves proxies for something protected. **(A1)**

**(d)** A defensible action is to **set the decision threshold separately for each area so that the false-positive rates are equalised**, and to publish the resulting precision and recall for both areas. **(A1)** This directly addresses the complaint, which is about unequal burden rather than about overall accuracy, and it is achievable within fixed inspection capacity because lowering the threshold in the North and raising it in the South reallocates roughly the same number of visits. **(A1)**

It must be accompanied by a stated decision about which error the authority considers more serious. If a missed urgent repair is the greater harm, the threshold should be set to favour recall and the authority must accept more minor inspections in both areas; if unnecessary visits are the greater harm, the reverse. **(A1)** What is not defensible is to continue reporting only the aggregate figure, because that suppresses exactly the information needed to make the choice.
questions.markscheme_notes: (a) The mark scheme looks for the idea that an aggregate conceals distribution, and for the identification of precision and recall (or the two error rates) as the disaggregated quantities. A candidate who says only that the model is biased has asserted a conclusion the data do not yet support. (b) Award (M1) for deriving at least one cell correctly from the text, since the numbers are given as counts of flagged and correctly flagged rather than as a matrix. Accept matrices with rows and columns transposed. All six rates must appear; the wrongly-flagged proportion is the one most often omitted and is the rate the complaint is actually about. (c) The comparison mark requires the ratio. Credit the observation that South recall is higher, because it prevents the easy conclusion that the model is simply worse in the South. The 'does not establish' mark is for the point that the statistics cannot separate miscalibration from threshold choice, or for noting that different base rates alone can produce this pattern. (d) Any single action is acceptable provided it is justified against the figures and acknowledges the trade-off. Equalising false-positive rates, equalising recall, or setting thresholds from an explicit cost ratio for the two error types are all creditable. An answer that proposes collecting more data or retraining without addressing the threshold question has not engaged with the fact that the trade-off is irreducible at fixed capacity.
questions.explanation:
The central move in this question is to refuse the aggregate. The authority's 82 percent overall precision is arithmetically correct and almost useless, because it averages over two areas that contribute requests in a three-to-one ratio, so it largely describes the North. Disaggregating produces a genuinely uncomfortable result: the South has better recall but far worse precision, and a non-urgent request there is more than four times as likely to trigger a visit. That is precisely the experience the tenant describes, so her complaint is not anecdote against statistics; it is the statistics, correctly computed.

The question is deliberately constructed so that the easy conclusion is wrong. It would be natural to read the figures as showing that the model discriminates against the South, but recall there is in fact higher. What differs is the threshold's effect in a population with a different base rate of urgency: 25 percent in the North against 20 percent in the South. A single threshold applied to two groups with different base rates produces different error mixes even when the underlying model is equally good in both, which is why the data cannot by themselves tell you whether the model is miscalibrated or merely being used at the wrong operating point. Recognising that distinction is the difference between a technical fix and a political one.

The final part is unavoidable because precision and recall trade off against each other and inspection capacity is fixed, so no amount of modelling removes the choice. Someone has to decide whether a missed urgent repair or an unnecessary visit is the worse failure, and that decision is a judgement about harm rather than a result about accuracy. The only clearly indefensible position is the authority's current one, of reporting a single number that conceals the fact that the choice is being made and being made unevenly. A student who reaches that conclusion has understood why the ethical content of this topic is not an addendum to the technical material but a consequence of it.

provenance.adaptation: Original case study. The confusion counts were chosen so that overall precision is a respectable 82 percent while one area's false-positive rate is more than four times the other's, and so that the worse-precision area has the better recall, which blocks the conclusion that the model is simply worse there.

verification.method: Confusion matrices recomputed in Python from the stated counts. North: TP 1080, FP 120, FN 420, TN 4380, precision 90.0 percent, recall 72.0 percent, wrongly flagged 2.67 percent. South: TP 320, FP 180, FN 80, TN 1420, precision 64.0 percent, recall 80.0 percent, wrongly flagged 11.25 percent. Overall precision 1400/1700 = 82.35 percent. Ratio of wrongly-flagged rates 4.22.
solution_skeleton: argue that an aggregate over unequal group sizes conceals the distribution of errors
build the confusion matrix for each group from the stated counts
compute precision, recall and the rate of wrongly flagged non-cases for each group
compare the error rates and identify what the comparison cannot establish
justify a threshold decision by naming which error type is judged more harmful

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Read the overall precision of 82 per cent, judge the model acceptable, and recommend that it be deployed across all areas.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The aggregate hides rates that differ by a factor of four between areas, and the area that complains has better recall at much worse precision, so the burden of the model's errors falls unequally on the groups it serves.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: Deployment recommended on the headline figure, with no per-area confusion matrices and no acknowledgement that which error to minimise is a value judgement rather than a calculation.
